newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, orange juice and oil prices rise.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, orange juice and oil prices rise.

text.p: Coffee futures roared ahead for a seventh straight day Wednesday on supply worries, and orange juice prices also rose as traders awaited news about a freeze in Florida citrus groves last weekend.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee prices set life-of-contract highs across the board as the market responded to a port strike in Colombia and reports of smaller crops to come in major producers Brazil and Mexico.
March coffee jumped to a high of 137.05 cents a pound before settling at 135.30 cents a pound, up 5.65 cents. The contract has risen 32 cents or 30 percent since its close on Dec. 6.
"This is still a reflection of underlying bullishness linked to a tight situation," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "It will persist if the Brazil crop comes in lower, as most people suggest."

At Buenaventura, Colombia's leading coffee port, striking dockworkers resumed talks with government officials and cargo handling operators to resolve an 8-day strike that has blocked shipment of more than 300,000 bags of coffee.

Preliminary forecasts by the Brazilian government have pegged the 1997/98 coffee crop in that country, the top exporter, at 18 to 20 million bags, compared with an estimated 25 million bags a year earlier.

Sparking additional buying was a report from broker Merrill Lynch suggesting the tight supply situation could drive prices as high as $2 a pound by mid-year. "Total supplies have not been this tight in 20 years," it said.

At the New York Cotton Exchange, frozen concentrate orange juice futures closed higher with March up 0.20 cent a pound at 86.85 cents with traders awaiting estimates of crop damage in Florida from last weekend's freezing cold.

Growers group Florida Citrus Mutual said a reliable estimate of losses remains several days away. But Bernard Savaiko, an analyst with Paine Webber, predicted about 10 percent of the crop suffered freeze damage.
Supplies still look sufficient in the long run, he said, based on a record U.S. crop, a possible record Brazilian crop, and a strong dollar, which hits exports to Europe and Japan.
March cocoa futures fell to a new contract low of $1,287 per metric ton before ending at $1,290, down $35 or nearly 3 percent, on the day as speculators and chart-watching fund traders sold heavily.
Traders also cited plentiful stocks from last year's big world crop as a continuing weight on the market.

Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast said projections of a smaller 1996/97 Ivory Coast cocoa crop coupled with lower production in Ghana, Malaysia and other producers could point to a supply deficit in the future.
"I would be surprised if it broke $1,280 without some fundamental reason," said Prendergast.
At the New York Mecantile Exchange, heating oil prices rose on expectations that weekly oil inventory data would show a decline in stocks following last week's frigid temperatures.
February heating oil ended up 0.86 cent at 66.89 cents a gallon.

In the data released by the American Petroleum Institute after the close of trading, stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel, fell 2.95 million barrels to 122.50 million in the week ended Jan. 17, in line with analyst expectations for a drop of three million barrels.
"The action was due to API expectations," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst with Cargill Investor Services Inc.
February gasoline ended up 0.78 cent to 68.22 cents a gallon, and March crude oil 2 cents higher at $24.24 a barrel.
The API also said crude oil stocks fell 3.42 million barrels last week, while gasoline stocks rose 3.03 million barrels.
Traders shrugged off a fire at Tosco Corp.'s Avon refinery in California on Tuesday.

"This rally was partly news driven by the Tosco fire but a West Coast refinery like this really doesn't have anything to do with the East Coast product market," said Al Lindseth, manager of oil and gas hedge programmes at GSC Energy in Atlanta.
